To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic ingestion of low doses of cadmium causes a marked decrease in the amount of zinc in the cytosol of male and female liver, and that the decrease occurs in the zinc metalloprotein regions of the protein profiles before the formation of metallothionin is detectable.

1) the low molecular weight zinc region is of importance in normal zinc metabolism and is not a cadmium-binding region; 2) the high molecular weight region is not a metallothionein binding region, although it is a zinc-binding region; and 3) there are significant quantitative differences between the cytosol zinc profiles of male and female rat livers.

(1) the cytosolic protein profiles of male and female rat livers are different in control animals and that (2) the cytosol protein profile changes of cadmium-exposed rats are dose related and are different in male and female animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cadmium and cadmium-zinc interactions in male and female liver cytosol proteins.
the effects of low oral doses of cadmium chloride on the zinc and cadmiium-containing protein profiles of male and female rat cytosol.
cadmium-induced changes in the zinc and/or cadmium-containing protein profiles of rat liver cytosols.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes induced by cadmium are not only quantitatively different between males and females but also that they occur at different times.

the cytosol zinc profile of the male rat liver was more sensitive than that of the female to the effects of cadmium ingestion, and that cadmium metallothionein formation was more extensive in the female than in the male rat liver.
the zinc and cadadium cytosol profiles of rat liver were altered in a manner that was dose and sex related.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the zinc and cadmiun metalloprotein profiles are altered by cadmium ingestion in both male and female rats, and that the changes are dose related, but the profiles differ quantitatively between males and females exposed chronically to cadmium chloride.
the cytosol zinc profile of the rat liver was disturbed by the presence of cadmium in a dose-related manner, and that this was reflected by the formation of cadmium-containing cytosol proteins.
cadmium exposure causes a dose-related decrease in zinc-containing protein and increases in the cadmium-containing protein profile of rat liver cytosols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the low molecular weight region is an important component of the zinc-containing cytosol proteins of the control rat liver and that this region is affected by the ingestion of low doses of cadmium.
the changes in zinc profile precede the changes in metallothionein and that the changes are dose related.

the changes in the zinc and the cadmium metalloproteins of rat liver cytosols obtained by Sephadex G-75 chromatography are dose related and that the low molecular weight zinc-containing cytosol fraction (3500 daltons), which is a newly identified zinc-containing fraction in rat liver cytools, is also cadmium containing.
